messages.author: 2d974991cab5f3a7
messages.subject: removing the loop
parts:
Dear All,
Hi,

Can I substitute the vectorized code instead of below loop to perform fast simulation?

vector logfunc(int n, vector x, real mu, real sigma)
    {
    real G;
    G = 0;
    for(i in 1:n)
        {
        G = G + log( normal_log(x[i],mu,sigma) + normal_cdf(x[i],mu,sigma) );
        }
    return G;
    }

Thanks in advance.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] removing the loop
parts:
I don't know why you'd want to add an expression the log
scale to one on the linear scale. Using Stan's latest notation
(and you don't want to use 2.10 due to a bug, only 2.11), did you
really mean:

G = G + normal_lpdf(x[i] | mu, sigma) + normal_lcdf(x[i] | mu, sigma)

Assuming n = rows(x) and you intended to add on the log scale, you can replace

logfunc(n, x, mu, sigma)

with the expression

normal_lpdf(x | mu, sigma) + normal_lcdf(x | mu, sigma)

And unless you want to be able to call the function with n != rows(x),
you don't want to pass in redundant arguments.

But then I don't see why you'd be adding a CDF term, either, especially
evaluated at the same point x[i] ---are you
trying to do upper-bound truncation by hand by any chance? If so,
you want to subtract the log CDF evaluated at the truncation point.
That you will need to multiply by n because there's only one truncation
point, unless that also varies by observation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: removing the loop
parts:
I work in the new distribution field. I want to check the Bayesian estimator by Stan. In fact I need to optimize similar previous and below code. I need speed and want to avoid 'for' in my logfunc function.

    functions
        {
        vector logfunc(int n, vector x, real alpha, real theta, real mu, real sigma)
            {
            vector[2] ret;
            real G;
            ret[1] = 0;
            ret[2] = 0;
            for(i in 1:n)
                {
                G = normal_cdf(x[i], mu, sigma);
                ret[1] = ret[1] + log(1-pow(G,theta));
                ret[2] = ret[2] + log( pow(G,alpha)+pow(1-pow(G,theta),alpha) );
                }
            return ret;           
            }
        }
    data
        {
        int<lower=1> n;
        vector[n] x;
        }
    parameters
        {
        real<lower=0> alpha;
        real<lower=0> theta;
        real mu;
        real<lower=0> sigma;
        }
    model
        {
        vector[2] retu;
        retu = logfunc(n, x, alpha, theta, mu, sigma);
        alpha ~ gamma(0.001,0.001);
        theta ~ gamma(0.001,0.001);
        sigma ~ gamma(0.001,0.001);
        mu ~ normal(0,100);
       
        target +=  n*log(theta) + normal_lpdf(x| mu, sigma) + (theta-1)*normal_lcdf(x | mu, sigma) + (alpha-1)*retu[1] - retu[2] ;
        }
       
Best
Bistoon

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] removing the loop
parts:
I'm afraid that function can't be vectorized. And we strongly
disrecommend those diffuse gamma priors for reasons discussed in
the manual and Andrew's papers.

I'd rewrite it as follows for arithmetic stability and efficiency
(and for formatting) as follows:

vector logfunc(vector x, real alpha, real theta, real mu, real sigma) {
vector[2] ret;
ret[1] = rep_vector(0, 2);
for(i in 1:rows(x)) {
real log_G;
real log1m_pow_G_theta;
log_G = normal_lcdf(x[i] | mu, sigma);
log1m_pow_G_theta = log1m(pow(exp(log_G), theta));
ret[1] = ret[1] + log1m_pow_G_theta;
ret[2] = ret[2] + log_sum_exp(alpha * log_G
alpha * log1m_pow_G_theta);
}
return ret;
}

I removed the redundant n parameter and used rows(x). I defined variables
closer to where they're being used in the loop (no loss in
efficiency, and only minor loss if they're containers).

The point is to work on the log scale wherever possible and
store intermediate calculations so as not to repeat them and
use built-ins for stability like log1m(u) instead of log(1 - u).
The built-ins are faster and more arithmetically stable.
Especially log_sum_exp, because it lets you prolong how long you
work on the log scale.

I still don't think this is optimal, and you should check my
algebra.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] removing the loop
parts:
I didn't think it would be much faster, just more
arithmetically stable (assumig I did the algebra right).
It's hard to measure speed across different runs with MCMC
because all the algorithms are probabilistic and can vary
by a factor of two chain to chain.

See the chapter in the manual on user-defined functions on how
to add it. One warning, though---if you define the function with
an _lpdf suffix rather than _log, you can use it with sampling notation
but won't be able to use it as a function until 2.12---there was
a bug in the parser that caused it to fail (better than succeeding
and doing the wrong thing, at least).

- Bob
